opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, it was a really fun and quite formative period. Around 2012 to 2014, deep learning was just starting to show it could do real things. Richard was pushing hard on recursive neural networks, the idea that you could build up the meaning of a sentence compositionally with neural representations. Andrej was coming more from the vision side, working with Fei-Fei Li. There was a natural question: if we can get vector representations of sentences, and convolutional networks give us good representations of images, can we put them in the same space? Then you could retrieve images from sentences, or sentences from images.

In hindsight it was very much early days. The models were small, the datasets were small by today's standards, and a lot of the machinery was quite hand-built. We were using tree structures from parsers to drive the composition, which made sense to a linguist like me. The field then largely moved away from that toward sequence models and eventually transformers, which just learn the structure they need from lots of data.

But I think the core intuition held up well. Language and vision could share a representational space, and grounding language in perception was an important direction rather than a side curiosity. You can draw a fairly direct line from that kind of work to image captioning, which Andrej went on to do some very nice work on, and eventually to things like CLIP and today's multimodal models. We didn't have the scale to make it work at that level, but the questions were the right ones.

It was also a great time just in terms of people. Stanford had this unusual mix of NLP, vision, and machine learning people all close together, and students moved between groups pretty freely. Richard and Andrej were both extremely energetic and ambitious. They each went on to have big influence, Richard with MetaMind and later work, and Andrej at OpenAI and Tesla and as an educator. So I look back on it fondly, as an early seed of where the field has gone.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I look back on it quite fondly, and honestly with a bit of amazement at how much came out of a fairly small group of people in a short window. This was roughly 2011 through 2014 or 2015, and at the time the idea of applying neural networks to natural language processing was still pretty unfashionable. Most of the field was deeply invested in feature engineering and discrete probabilistic models, and a lot of people thought the neural stuff was a fad that had already been tried and failed in the nineties.

Richard was really the one who pulled me into it. He arrived at Stanford very enthusiastic about deep learning, and he started working with Andrew Ng and me together. The early work was things like recursive neural networks for parsing and sentiment, and then the natural extension was: if you can build a vector representation for a sentence, and people on the vision side are building vector representations for images, why not try to put them in the same space? So we did work on zero-shot learning, where you could describe an object class in words and recognize images of it even though you'd never seen a labeled example. And then grounded compositional semantics, mapping sentences and images into a joint embedding space so you could retrieve one from the other.

Andrej then took that direction much further. He came in a bit later, worked with Fei-Fei Li as his main advisor, but there was a lot of cross-pollination between our groups. The image captioning work he did, where you generate descriptions of images region by region, that was genuinely one of the results that made people outside the field sit up and realize something had changed. It wasn't just classification anymore. The model was producing language about the world.

What strikes me in hindsight is that the ingredients we were playing with turned out to be the right ones, even though the scale was tiny. Dense vector representations, learning everything end to end, joint embedding spaces across modalities. That's essentially the conceptual skeleton of what CLIP and the modern multimodal models do, just with orders of magnitude more data and compute. We were doing it with a few thousand images and the word vectors we could train on a desktop.

The other thing I'd say is that I think I was slower than Richard and Andrej to believe how far it would go. They had the conviction of young people who weren't carrying around the baggage of what had been tried before. I was more cautious, more inclined to think there'd be a ceiling. I was wrong about where the ceiling was, and I've tried to take that lesson to heart since.

And it's been a pleasure watching what they've both done. Richard with his company and Salesforce research, Andrej at OpenAI and Tesla and his teaching, which has reached far more people than any paper we wrote. Having students who end up shaping the field is the best outcome an advisor can hope for.

astra-6.text:
I look back on that as a really exciting period. We were interested in how you could connect language to the visual world, rather than treating language as something that exists entirely on its own. Richard and Andrej both brought tremendous energy to that question.

A lot of the challenge was figuring out how to represent the two modalities so that they could interact. You have an image and a sentence, but you’d like to do more than say that they match. You’d like to connect particular words or phrases with particular parts of the image. That gives you a way to think about describing images, but also about grounding the meaning of language.

Looking back, I think the direction was very fruitful, even though the systems were much more limited than what we have today. There’s something wonderful about working with students who take a broad research question and develop it in directions you wouldn’t have anticipated yourself.

sol-6.1.text:
I look back on it very fondly. Richard and Andrej were interested in how you could connect language to the visual world, and that seemed like a very natural direction. So much of what we talk about concerns things we see, yet language processing and computer vision had largely developed as separate communities.

One of the central ideas was to learn representations that let you bring images and language together. Could you associate parts of a sentence with regions of an image? Could you move from recognizing objects to describing what was happening? That led into work on image descriptions and image captioning.

In retrospect, those were early steps toward the multimodal systems we have today. But I wouldn’t want to suggest that we had the whole trajectory mapped out. There were interesting problems, the neural network methods were starting to work, and Richard and Andrej had tremendous energy for pursuing them.
